contributions.headingText: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) associated with chronic inflammation (CI-DLBCL) is an EBV-associated neoplasm occurring in the setting of longstanding chronic inflammation involving confined natural body spaces or acquired tissue spaces. Pyothorax-associated lymphoma (PAL) is the prototypical form, developing in the pleural cavity of patients with longstanding pyothorax.
9680/3 Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma associated with chronic inflammation
2A81.7 Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma associated with chronic inflammation
The most frequently reported sites are the pleural cavity, bone (especially the femur), joints, and periarticular soft tissue {15897752}.

Symptoms of PAL include chest and back pain; fever; and respiratory symptoms, such as cough, haemoptysis, and dyspnoea. Radiological examination reveals a tumour mass in the pleura (in 80% of cases), pleura and lung, or lung near the pleura. Serum LDH is commonly elevated {12023576; 12377970}. CI-DLBCL lesions in the bone, joint, periarticular soft tissue, or skin usually present with pain and/or a mass lesion. The involved bone shows lytic lesions.

PAL develops after a long history (median: 37 years) of pyothorax, often resulting from artificial pneumothorax for the treatment of tuberculosis {12023576; 12377970; 16330929; 17043091}. As this procedure is no longer practised, the incidence of PAL has drastically decreased. Cases have been reported mostly in Japan, and rarely elsewhere. Patient age at diagnosis ranges from the fifth to eighth decade of life {12377970; 17043091}. The M:F ratio is 12:1 {8001926; 12023576}.

For CI-DLBCL arising in other settings, such as chronic osteomyelitis, metallic implant insertion, surgical mesh implantation, and chronic skin venous ulcer, the interval following the predisposing event is usually > 10 years (range: 1.2–57 years) {9422983; 15897752; 18801089}.
CI-DLBCL develops in patients without recognized immunodeficiency, with the possible exception of immunosenescence {9778104; 33564306}.

CI-DLBCL is strongly associated with EBV infection {8238246; 12023576; 14556658; 16385574}. Chronic inflammation in a confined space probably induces local immunodeficiency by the production of IL-10, favouring escape from immunosurveillance of EBV-transformed B cells, which are also stimulated via autocrine or paracrine IL-6R engagement {8765317; 9209445; 9422983; 15897752}.

Immunoglobulin genes are clonally rearranged and hypermutated but lack ongoing mutations {12065872; 18079737}. Cytogenetics show complex karyotypes with numerous abnormalities {14556658}. TP53 mutations are found in about 70% of cases {9515788}. TNFAIP3 (A20) is often deleted {23418597}.

The gene expression profile of PAL is distinct from that of nodal DLBCL, at least partly due to EBV infection {15504251}. Downregulation of HLA class I expression and mutations of cytotoxic T-lymphocyte epitopes in EBNA3B might contribute to the immune escape of lymphoma cells {10417757; 11058881}. The latter process also involves regulatory T cells, which are abundantly present in PAL {30953706}.
PAL lesions are usually large (often > 100 mm). Few data, however, exist for CI-DLBCL at other sites {16330929}.

Most cases show a centroblastic or immunoblastic morphology, with round nuclei and large nucleoli {31735345; 31863183}. Massive necrosis and angiocentric growth may be present.

Immunophenotype

Most cases express B-lineage markers, such as CD20 and CD79a. Some cases may show plasmablastic differentiation, manifesting as variable loss of CD20 and/or CD79a, and variable expression of IRF4 (MUM1) and CD138. Lymphoma cells exhibit an activated B-cell–like phenotype. CD30 may be expressed. Occasional cases aberrantly express one or more T-cell antigens (CD2, CD3, CD4, CD7), causing problems in lineage assignment {12023576; 12377970}. Type III EBV latency (i.e. positivity for LMP1 and EBNA2) is characteristic {12023576; 18801089}.

Differential diagnosis

Cases showing plasmablastic differentiation must be distinguished from plasmablastic lymphoma on the basis of clinical context. CI-DLBCL and fibrin-associated large B-cell lymphoma (FA-LBCL) have overlapping cytological and phenotypic features. Their distinction, however, is important because of the aggressive nature of CI-DLBCL compared with the rather indolent nature of FA-LBCL. At least focal infiltration in pre-existing structures or the formation of a mass lesion distinguishes CI-DLBCL from FA-LBCL. Fibrin deposits are common in FA-LBCL but rare in CI-DLBCL. The distinction between the two is especially difficult, if possible at all, on small specimens such as core needle biopsies. Clinicopathological correlations and imaging studies are highly contributory to making the distinction.

PAL differs from primary effusion lymphoma, which is KSHV/HHV8-positive and in most cases presents with effusions in the absence of a tumour mass.
The diagnosis is very difficult to make on FNAB and requires ancillary methods.
In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded small RNA (EBER) is positive in tumour cells.

Essential: large B-cell lymphoma; setting of local chronic inflammation; EBV association; exclusion of other EBV-associated neoplasms.

Desirable: occurrence in a natural or acquired confined body or tissue space.
CI-DLBCL is staged according to the Lugano classification {25113753}. PAL tumours are often confined to the thoracic cavity at diagnosis {12377970}.

CI-DLBCL is an aggressive lymphoma. The 5-year overall survival rate of PAL is 20–35% {12377970; 17043091}. Poor performance status, high LDH levels, and high clinical stage are unfavourable factors {17043091}. Outcome data are limited for CI-DLBCL other than PAL.
